noncomputable abbrev r := Set.IsAPOfLengthFree.maxCard

/--
Prove an asymptotic formula for $r_k(N)$, the largest possible size of a subset
of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ that does not contain any non-trivial $k$-term arithmetic progression.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_142 (k : ℕ) : (fun N => (r k N : ℝ)) =Θ[atTop] (answer(sorry) : ℕ → ℝ) := by
  sorry

/--
Show that $r_k(N) = o_k(N / \log N)$, where $r_k(N)$ the largest possible size of a subset
of $\{1, \dots, N\}$ that does not contain any non-trivial $k$-term arithmetic progression.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_142.variants.lower (k : ℕ) (hk : 1 < k) :
    (fun N => (r k N : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun N : ℕ => N / (N : ℝ).log) := by
  sorry


/--
Find functions $f_k$, such that $r_k(N) = O_k(f_k)$, where $r_k(N)$ the largest possible size of a

-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_142.variants.upper (k : ℕ) :
    (fun N => (r k N : ℝ)) =O[atTop] (answer(sorry) : ℕ → ℝ) := by

@[category research open, AMS 11]

end Erdos142

findings.description: The docstring asks for an asymptotic formula, but `=Θ[atTop]` only determines the order of magnitude, up to multiplicative constants. These are genuinely different requirements: the scratch file proves, for the actual r_k, that r_k = Θ(2r_k) while r_k is not asymptotically equivalent to 2r_k. This is classified as a documentation mismatch because the cited webpage explicitly also poses the weaker order-of-magnitude problem, which the Lean statement faithfully encodes.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/142 asks, in its main statement, to “Prove an asymptotic formula for r_k(N),” but separately says that [Er80] and [Va99] ask “(much more reasonably) for the order of magnitude.” Erdős, “On the combinatorial problems which I would most like to see solved,” §II.1, p.4 of https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1981-16.pdf, likewise distinguishes improving the bounds from obtaining an asymptotic formula.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to “Determine the order of magnitude of r_k(N)” and identify it as the weaker sourced formulation. If the stronger asymptotic-formula problem is intended, instead use `Asymptotics.IsEquivalent atTop (fun N => (r k N : ℝ)) (answer(sorry) : ℕ → ℝ)`, retaining the Θ statement as a separate variant.

findings.description: As with the general theorem, the docstring advertises an asymptotic formula for r_3, whereas the Lean statement asks only for its order of magnitude. Specializing to k = 3 does not eliminate the distinction between Θ-equivalence and asymptotic equivalence. The mathematics is supported by the source's weaker order-of-magnitude formulation, so correcting the description is sufficient if that is the intended variant.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/142 says “An asymptotic formula is still far out of reach, even for k=3,” and separately discusses the order-of-magnitude problem. In §II.1 of https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1981-16.pdf, Erdős explicitly asks to obtain “an asymptotic formula for r_3(n) and more generally for r_k(n).”
findings.suggested_fix: Describe this as determining the order of magnitude of r_3(N). Alternatively, to state the asymptotic-formula request, replace Θ with `Asymptotics.IsEquivalent` (notation `~[atTop]` with the appropriate scope).

reformulations.difference: The source describes a largest progression-free subset. Lean implements this using a natural-number supremum and encodes nontrivial progressions through set cardinality rather than an explicit positive common difference.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For k > 1, a progression set of cardinality k cannot have difference zero; conversely, a positive difference produces k distinct natural-number terms. The scratch file proves `free_iff_no_positive_step`. The candidate cardinalities include zero and are bounded by N, so the supremum is attained, not a default value. `r_eq_iff_maximum` proves the exact maximum characterization, and `maximum_correct` identifies r with a computable finite enumeration. Boundary checks include r_k(0)=0, r_0(N)=r_1(N)=N, and r_2(N)=1 for N>0.

reformulations.difference: The declaration includes the elementary case k=2, whereas the substantive source discussion starts at k=3; its functions also use totalized real logarithm and division on all natural inputs.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The added case is true: r_2(N)=1 for N>0 and log(N)/N tends to zero. `lower_range_equivalence` proves the equivalence of the universally quantified statements over k>1 and k≥3. Also, N/log(N) is positive for N≥2, so the values at N=0,1 do not affect the atTop statement. `littleo_iff_scaled_tendsto` proves equivalence with r_k(N)·log(N)/N tending to zero.

review.notes: Checked all five declarations. No mathematical misformalization or stale status was found beyond the two documentation mismatches above. In particular, Θ is not equivalent to an asymptotic formula; it is acceptable here because the source separately poses the weaker problem. The upper-bound answer slot constrains its answer: N is a trivial majorant, but zero is not. I did not treat mathematically uninteresting answer choices as defects, following CONTRIBUTING.md. The function-valued answer expressions can depend on k. `/workspace/review/scratch.lean` compiles without errors or warnings, proves the definition and boundary-case checks without the problem's sorry theorems, and verifies finite enumeration through N=10. No repository files were edited.
